title: Who I am
job: Introduce yourself and state what you like

rules.text: Reflexive introductions: me llamo / te llamas — your name is what you call yourself.
The subject pronoun is usually dropped — the ending already says who: soy = I-am, quiero = I-want.
Every noun carries a gender, and the article agrees with it — el (m) · la (f) · los / las (plural).
gustar works backwards: the thing liked is the grammatical subject — "the coffee pleases me".

words.note: Reflexive — literally "I call myself". This, not "mi nombre", is how a name is given.

sentences.trap: "Mi nombre es…" is the English sentence translated word for word — grammatical, but nobody introduces themselves that way.
sentences.sound: ll sounds like the y in "yes" — me YAH-mo.

variations.changed: swap the name — Me llamo never changes
me → se: the same verb, a different person

mistake.why: No "es" — llamo is already the verb.

sentences.mnemonic: llamo = "I call (myself)" — your name is what you call yourself.

words.note: ser — the lasting "am": origin and identity. The "I" sits inside the ending.

sentences.trap: English has one "am"; Spanish has two. Where you are from is ser (soy), never estar.
sentences.sound: Soy rhymes with English "boy"; India opens with EEN-, not EYE-.

variations.changed: soy → eres: the ending swaps the person
soy → es — and still no pronoun in front

mistake.why: Drop the yo — soy already says "I am". Keep it only for contrast.

sentences.usage: Where you are from — the second or third line of any introduction.
sentences.mnemonic: ser = who you are, lastingly. Soy de India, not estoy.

words.note: Backwards from English: the coffee does the pleasing, so the verb follows the coffee — not you.
The article carries the noun's gender and number: el (m) · la (f) · los / las (plural).
Cognate, and masculine — so el café.

sentences.trap: "Yo gusto el café" copies the English shape — it says that you are the one doing the pleasing.
sentences.sound: Stress lands on the last syllable — ka-FEH, with a clipped final e.

variations.changed: café → agua — and it still takes el, though agua is feminine
Me → te: who is pleased changes, gusta does not

mistake.why: gustar runs backwards — the thing liked is the subject: Me gusta el café.

sentences.usage: Likes of every kind — food, music, people.
sentences.mnemonic: gustar = "to please" — English likes, Spanish pleases.

words.note: querer — wanting (and, later, loving). The "I" is inside the ending.
Feminine, yet it takes el in the singular — el agua. A famous quirk.

sentences.trap: "Yo quiero agua" is the English habit of always naming the subject; Spanish drops it unless it is drawing a contrast.
sentences.sound: agua is AH-gwa — the u is a glide, not a syllable of its own.

variations.changed: Quiero → quieres: the ending says who wants
add el — that particular coffee, not coffee in general

mistake.why: Drop the yo — quiero already means "I want".

sentences.usage: Asking for what you want — shops, tables, homes.
sentences.mnemonic: querer → Quiero: the -o ending is the "I".
